description: ATS UAQ Math & Robotics Team is building Mission Architect, a browser-based spacecraft-design game using real orbital mechanics (the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation) for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Our team of 5 Grade 12 students, mentored by teachers Ahmed El Deeb and Bahaa Saleh, brings coding, bilingual EN/AR design, and a shared love of the UAE's space program (Hope probe, Rashid rover, Hazza Al Mansouri) to this build.
summary: Mission Architect is a browser-based spacecraft design game where players choose a destination (LEO, the Moon, or Mars), then balance propulsion, power, propellant mass, and scientific instruments against real orbital-mechanics constraints before launching and seeing whether the mission actually succeeds. The physics engine is built on the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, using real specific-impulse figures for chemical and nuclear-thermal (NASA DRACO-class) propulsion, inverse-square solar power falloff, and MMRTG-class radioisotope power, scaled to real Moon and Mars mission requirements. The scoring model penalizes both under- and over-designed spacecraft, so players feel the same mass, power, and propellant trade-offs real mission architects face. Built with HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge Space Mission Design Game, by the ATS UAQ Math & Robotics Team in Umm Al Quwain, with a bilingual English/Arabic mission report.
details:
Mission Architect is a browser-based spacecraft design and mission-planning game built for Umm Al Quwain students to turn abstract physics into a hands-on decision: pick a destination (Low Earth Orbit, the Moon, or Mars), then design a spacecraft within real mass, power, and propulsion trade-offs before launching it and seeing whether the mission actually succeeds.

Every choice feeds a physics engine built on the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation and real propulsion/power data. Propulsion options range from chemical engines to a Nuclear Thermal Propulsion (NTP) engine modeled on NASA's DRACO program, each with its own specific impulse. Power sources include solar panels (whose output falls off with the inverse square of distance from the Sun, exactly as it does for real spacecraft) and a Multi-Mission Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator (MMRTG) modeled on the unit that powers NASA's Mars rovers, which supplies steady power regardless of distance or sunlight. Destination requirements (delta-v, distance, trip time, and risk) are scaled from real mission data for the Moon and Mars. The scoring engine penalizes both under- and over-designed spacecraft: too little propellant and the mission fails outright; far too much propellant for the propulsion type, and efficiency and feasibility scores collapse instead, nudging players toward the same trade-offs real mission architects face.

The game was built with HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript, with no external game engine or framework, so it runs instantly in any browser with no installation. We used AI (Super Intelligence) tools to help brainstorm the mission-design concept, research the real propulsion and power figures and mission constraints that ground the physics model, debug the scoring logic, and edit and translate our written text (including the bilingual Arabic/English toggle in the final mission report). The game's core physics formulas, UI, and content were authored and tuned by our team. Our demo video's background music and title/credit cards were generated with AI assistance; this is acknowledged in the video's own on-screen text and file metadata.

Built by the ATS UAQ Math & Robotics Team for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, Umm Al Quwain Local Event.
